stories.title: Sudan farms lie barren as El Nino leaves Nile banks dry
stories.summary: Along the bone-dry riverbanks of the Nile in Sudan, farmers struggle to pull water to their crops. Others gather to pray for rainfall over cracked earth. Across the country, farmland that could feed the world's largest hunger crisis many times over lies fallow, as weary farmers once again find themselves in the crosshairs of faraway destruction. First came war between the country's army and rival paramilitaries, which since April 2023 has killed more than 200,000 people and pushed nearly 20 million into crisis levels of hunger. Then a more distant conflict, between Iran and the United States, crippled fuel and fertiliser supply through the Strait of Hormuz, causing costs to soar. And now the powerful El Nino climate pattern strengthening in the Pacific Ocean, which impacts winds and rains across the world, has delayed crucial rains and led water levels in the life-giving Nile to drop precipitously. Just south of the capital Khartoum, farmer Al-Tigani Fadlallah points to an island that shouldn't be there. "The water usually covers it by July, but you can see it even now," he told AFP this month, seeing in the sunbaked sandbank a bad omen for his parched crops. Through the length of Sudan, from the northern fields near Egypt, along the Nile river to the Ethiopian border, farmers told AFP reporters the water they need is not rising from the riverbanks nor falling from the sky. The UN's food and agriculture organisation says the season "is unfolding under heightened climate risk, driven by El Nino conditions" including delayed and below average rains, and long and frequent dry spells. Farmers say it is one of the hardest seasons in recent memory, but climate research shows it will not be the last. Climate and hydrology scientist Elfatih Eltahir, at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has studied the link between El Nino and the Nile for thirty years.

stories.title: Is Trump making Latin America great again?
stories.summary: A right-wing wave is sweeping through the region and that is not good news. The calamitous war on Iran and continuing failure to rein in Israel have brought United States President Donald Trump collapsing approval ratings and growing public animosity at home. Yet there is one area of his foreign policy that is perhaps serving as a consolation: Latin America. Over the past year and a half, a slew of right-wing leaders has taken power in the region through electoral victories for which Trump has more or less taken personal credit. These leaders appear eager to facilitate the resurgence of US power projection in what Trump has, with characteristic pompousness, called the “Donroe Doctrine”. This, to put it mildly, is not great news for the average Latin American. One need only glance at the extensive history of US collaboration with right-wing Latin American regimes in the ostensible fight against leftist politics and “narco-terror” to assume that what is coming will entail a whole lot of civilian casualties. In Colombia, for example, where far-right millionaire businessman and former criminal defence lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella was just sworn in, the US track record of funnelling heaps of money to a homicidal army joined at the hip with right-wing paramilitary outfits produced a good deal of bloodshed. And what do you know: De la Espriella amassed a portion of his lawyerly fortune defending paramilitary leaders. In addition to having charmingly pledged to “disembowel” the left, de la Espriella is obsessed with jumpstarting fracking and pursuing other environmentally destructive projects. Trump’s posse of Latin American acolytes also includes the likes of Argentina’s Javier Milei, the uniquely coiffed chainsaw-wielding character whose party did smashingly in October midterm elections after Trump conditioned a $40bn bailout of the country on just such an outcome at the polls. Milei’s decision to wipe out welfare provisions has sent millions of Argentinians into poverty and flooded the streets of Buenos Aires with homeless people.

stories.title: Lavrov sees West fighting against Russia, using `bodies’ of Ukrainian regime
stories.summary: The West is being busy pumping the Kiev regime with weapons, Russian Foreign Minister said
article_sentences: MOSCOW, August 22.
The West is waging its war on Russia, using Ukrainians’ bodies, itself being busy pumping the Kiev regime with weapons, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
"Indeed, the West, which is currently fighting against us, as they say, using `the Ukrainian regime’s hands’, [is] mostly [doing so,] using the Ukrainian regime’s bodies.
While the West’s hands are busy pumping this anti-people regime with weapons and advanced technology," Russia’s top diplomat said in an interview with Vesti television on Saturday.

stories.title: West welcome to join work on Eurasian security without connivance with Brussels — Lavrov
stories.summary: MOSCOW, August 22. Russia will be happy if countries in western Eurasia can join the work to ensure the continent’s security, but only if Europe refuses connivance with the interests of bureaucrats in Brussels alone, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told Vesti television in an interview on Saturday. Countries across entire Eurasia are invited to take part in efforts to build a continental security architecture, he emphasized. "When the western part of the continent <…> opts for those who care for national interests, rather than the interests of bureaucrats in Brussels, we will certainly be happy if they can join the processes that I mentioned," Lavrov maintained.
